hypotheses.hypothesis: As politics becomes more central to personal identity, coverage should increasingly use identity-and-tribalism vocabulary, which should rise over time and signal a shift toward politics being rated 'very important'.
Coverage of Congress is likely to carry more gridlock and disengagement framing over time, which would reflect declining personal investment in politics (direction A).
Early-period framing of politics as bipartisan and consensual should give way to adversarial 'us versus them' framing in later coverage, indicating rising personal stakes (direction B).
Coverage of opinion polls should shift from treating poll numbers as meaningful to dismissing them, suggesting that politics is seen as less relevant to ordinary people (direction A).
Voting-access coverage (mail ballots, early voting, ID rules) should increasingly report long waits and crowded polls, reflecting heightened public investment in voting (direction B).
Coverage of material hardship that damages physical health (cold homes, damp, or going without essentials) rises over the period, so self-rated health should drift toward 'Very poor' (Direction A).

Early-period coverage centres on lockdown-era confinement, while late-period coverage centres on people recovering their strength and feeling physically restored, implying a shift toward 'Very good' (Direction B).

Coverage of everyday self-care (sleep, diet, supplements) with reports of feeling more energetic and losing weight increases, consistent with self-rated health moving toward 'Very good' (Direction B).

In screening and check-ups, early coverage emphasises timely detection and rising uptake, while late coverage emphasises cancelled appointments and delayed diagnosis, pointing toward 'Very poor' (Direction A).

Coverage of sports, outdoor exercise and fitness events grows as people report returning to activity, so self-rated health should move toward 'Very good' (Direction B). Note this differs from the earlier gym/parkrun test by focusing on team sports and outdoor recreation.

If average membership status moved toward 'Not a member', coverage should show rising use of the survey-style phrase 'no religious preference' and related self-identification language, which is more distinctive than the 'unaffiliated' terms already tested.

If the shift was toward 'Active member', youth programming coverage should move from dropout and closure framing to enrollment growth framing.

If average status moved toward 'Not a member', coverage should show more explicit reports of people ceasing attendance and dropping affiliation, using plain-language phrasing that is more specific than the earlier 'left the church' type terms.
Coverage of football clubs increasingly reports players re-registering or returning to their clubs, which would indicate a rising share of active membership (Direction A).
Coverage of informal five-a-side and walking football increasingly describes players who take part without any club affiliation, which would indicate a rising share of non-members (Direction B).
Football coverage shifts from informal, unaffiliated play toward formal registered and affiliated club membership, which would indicate movement toward active membership (Direction A).

Coverage of bowls and athletics clubs shifts from describing affiliated, paying members toward describing resignations and lapsed affiliation, which would indicate movement toward non-membership (Direction B).

Coverage increasingly cites the cost of playing sport, such as affordability of subscriptions and fees, as a reason people stop belonging to clubs, which would indicate a rising share of non-members (Direction B).
Coverage of arts and music groups increasingly describes people taking hands-on organizational roles (running events, sitting on boards, crewing productions), suggesting a rise in active membership.
Within coverage of youth and community performing groups, reports of members quitting or stopping dues should rise, signalling a shift toward non-membership.
Descriptions of people's relationship to arts and educational bodies move from active involvement language early to detached, unaffiliated language later, indicating a shift toward non-membership.

In coverage of hobby studios and workshops, early reports of sporadic or sign-up-only participation give way to later reports of committed weekly attendance, indicating a move toward active membership.
Membership language in arts and music organizations increasingly uses tiered, committed-member terms, which would accompany a rise in active rather than nominal membership.
Coverage of members walking away from a party in large numbers should rise if the share of people reporting non-membership grew.
Coverage of volunteer surges and record sign-ups to party campaigns should rise if active membership grew.
Within coverage of party membership, explicit resignation language should become more frequent if people increasingly left parties.
Descriptions of party supporters shifting from passive mailing-list or newsletter readers toward field-level organisers would indicate movement toward active membership.
Within coverage of party conferences, a shift from full delegate attendance to depleted ranks would signal a decline in engaged membership.
Coverage of civic disengagement and falling joiner rates should rise over time, reflecting a shift toward respondents reporting no membership in voluntary groups.
Coverage of large international relief charities should show more volunteer onboarding and hands-on participation language over time, consistent with a rise in active membership.
Engagement language should move from one-off, transactional giving toward recurring hands-on participation, consistent with a shift toward active membership.

In coverage of fraternal and lodge-based service groups, language about active initiation and lodge events should give way to language about lodges closing and members aging out, consistent with a shift toward non-membership.
Mentions of people no longer belonging to any group, or having given up memberships, should become more frequent over time, consistent with a shift toward non-membership.

Coverage of fair housing enforcement and anti-discrimination rental protections rises over time, reflecting growing public acceptance of neighbors of other races (Direction B: toward 'Not mentioned').
Among articles about housing and residential life, mentions of explicit racial exclusion in rentals and sales decline over time, consistent with a shift toward Direction B.

Discourse shifts from frank avowals of racial separation toward language of demographic anxiety and ethnic preservation, indicating more people willing to voice reluctance about different-race neighbors (Direction A: toward 'Mentioned').
In coverage of neighborhoods and tenants, early framing of racial exclusion as open policy gives way to 'diverse' and 'mixed-income' framing, pointing toward Direction B.
Reports of anti-Asian and anti-Latino harassment in residential settings increase, reflecting rising hostility toward neighbors of other races (Direction A: toward 'Mentioned').

As public discourse grows more comfortable with religious pluralism, coverage will increasingly use multifaith and pluralism vocabulary, which should track a shift toward greater willingness to live alongside people of other faiths (direction B).

Rising discomfort with religious change will show up as more coverage of cultural-heritage framing ("Great Replacement", "cultural erosion", "Christian heritage", "Judeo-Christian"), signalling a shift toward unwillingness to have neighbours of other faiths (direction A).
Coverage of non-Muslim minority houses of worship will increasingly describe friendly neighbourly contact, which should accompany a move toward accepting neighbours of other religions (direction B).

Framing shifts from a 'melting pot' or guest-worker vision of diversity toward a 'national culture' and 'Christian heritage' vision, indicating a move toward reluctance to accept different-faith neighbours (direction A).

Reporting on housing estates with Muslim residents shifts from describing peaceful coexistence to describing neighbour complaints and wariness, reflecting a move toward unwillingness to have different-faith neighbours (direction A).
Acceptance of unmarried couples rose, so coverage of unmarried-partner households using the census term POSSLQ and related household-classification language should increase.
Disapproval of unmarried couples as neighbors rose, so coverage of neighborhood nuisance and safety concerns should increase in its wording about who is a 'bad' neighbor.

Disapproval framing shifted from moral judgment of living together to concern about harm to children of cohabiting parents, which should appear as a move from early moral terms to later child-welfare terms.
In manufactured-housing communities, rules shifted from explicit marital requirements toward open-admission language, so the early-to-late balance should favor open-admission terms.
Disapproval of unmarried cohabitation rose alongside appeals to family stability, so coverage invoking two-parent household norms should increase.
Coverage of opportunistic theft and crimes against unsuspecting victims becomes more frequent over time, reflecting a growing sense that others will take advantage when given the chance.
Reporting on bystander and community helping behavior, such as stopping to aid strangers, increases over time, consistent with a shift toward perceiving others as fair.
Language describing openness toward others gives way to language of guardedness and self-protection, indicating a move toward believing others will take advantage.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In peer-to-peer marketplace and hosting coverage (rideshare, short-term rentals), descriptions shift from scam-oriented wording toward verified, trusted-user wording, consistent with a move toward believing people are fair.
Explicit statements giving others the benefit of the doubt and assuming good intentions become more common, signaling a rise in perceived fairness among people.
If average life satisfaction rose, news coverage should increasingly describe people as feeling better off and more secure, using distinctive upbeat phrasing about improved personal circumstances.
If satisfaction moved toward satisfied, coverage of inflation and household energy costs should shift toward reports of easing prices and falling bills.
If satisfaction moved toward dissatisfied, coverage should move from talk of rising real pay toward talk of squeezed incomes and falling living standards.
If satisfaction moved toward satisfied, rail and transport coverage should shift from disruption and cancellations toward restored services and frozen fares.

Coverage increasingly praises rule-following and playing it safe, so explicit rule-following phrases should rise over time, consistent with a shift toward 'Not at all like me' on creativity.
In banking coverage, compliance-oriented vocabulary should grow relative to new-product language, reflecting a move toward procedural conformity rather than creative thinking.

Leisure coverage should shift from passive consumption toward hands-on making, so maker and DIY vocabulary should replace spectator-style leisure language, pointing toward a rise in self-described creativity.
In cooking coverage, a move from pre-packaged food toward homemade experimentation should signal growing emphasis on personal creative expression.
Open-source and hands-on build culture has grown in coverage, so technical making terms should increase if the public places more value on creating new things.

Coverage of acute household hardship (bill shock, overdrafts, and reports of the worst conditions in decades) rises over the period, pointing toward a shift toward dissatisfaction with household finances.
Within grocery-shopping coverage, mentions of discounting and cheaper own-brand options rise, indicating households finding ways to stretch their budgets and feel more satisfied with their finances.
Language describing peak, runaway inflation gives way to language describing disinflation and stable prices, signalling a move toward household financial satisfaction.
In coverage of interest rates, early language about cheap, held-down borrowing costs shifts to late language about rate rises biting into household payments, indicating a move toward dissatisfaction.
Coverage of negotiated pay gains and wage settlements becomes more frequent, reflecting improved household incomes and a shift toward satisfaction with finances.
Coverage of family members betraying or deceiving one another will rise over time, reflecting weaker trust in relatives (Direction A).

hypotheses.hypothesis: If the average answer moved toward strong disagreement, coverage should mention out-of-school girls and the gender literacy gap less often over time, as girls' access becomes less of a public concern.
If the average answer moved toward strong agreement, coverage about schooling decisions should increasingly favour sons, using explicit son-first phrasing in education discussions.
If the answer moved toward strong disagreement, coverage should shift from language of women's subordinate household role to language of shared household decision-making.
If the answer moved toward strong agreement, discussion of paying for further study should move from fee waivers for women toward prioritising sons' tuition and family savings for male relatives.
If the answer moved toward strong agreement, coverage should increasingly endorse women's primary role as mothers and homemakers, using explicit stay-at-home framing.

As concern about workforce shortages grows, news coverage should increasingly stress recruitment failures and unfilled vacancies, reinforcing the view that work matters and that people stepping back is a problem.
Coverage of the cost-of-living squeeze on households should increasingly feature second jobs and extra hours, so work is framed as an economic necessity rather than an optional part of life.
Coverage shifting from a traditional work-centred vocabulary to language about purpose and fulfilment beyond employment would signal a move toward viewing reduced work emphasis as positive.

Among coverage of families and parents, a shift from dual-earner and career-focused language toward financial-strain language would indicate work being seen as a necessity whose reduced importance is a bad thing.
Coverage of alternative economic models such as degrowth and wellbeing economies should rise as a positive counterpoint to work-centred growth, reflecting favourable framing of less emphasis on work.
Coverage increasingly frames technology in terms of tangible personal benefits to daily life, so mentions of life-improving outcomes should rise, signalling a shift toward a 'Good thing' view.
Public unease about autonomous driving grows as high-profile crashes and regulatory probes attract coverage, so safety-failure language should increase, signalling a shift toward a 'Bad thing' view.

Quantum computing coverage shifts from aspirational 'race to build' framing to security-threat framing, so threat-related language should replace excitement-related language, signalling a 'Bad thing' shift.
Rising concern about security of digital infrastructure leads to more coverage of hostile intrusions into computer systems, signalling a shift toward a 'Bad thing' view of technological development.
Coverage moves from gloomy language about technological decline toward hopeful, forward-looking language about a new era, signalling a shift toward a 'Good thing' view.

If public attitudes move toward seeing greater respect for authority as a bad thing, coverage should increasingly use distinctly authoritarian-warning vocabulary, which is rare in ordinary discussion of order.

If attitudes move toward seeing respect for authority as a good thing, coverage of young people should increasingly frame them through moral-decline and discipline concerns, such as curfews and antisocial behaviour measures.

If attitudes move toward seeing greater respect for authority as a bad thing, the framing of deference should shift from traditional-values language to explicit warnings about dictators and autocratic rule.

If attitudes move toward seeing respect for authority as a good thing, coverage of politicians should shift from corruption and elite-distrust language toward stability and public-confidence language.

If attitudes move toward seeing respect for authority as a good thing, coverage should increasingly invoke social breakdown and the need for shared rules, using distinctive phrases about lost order and civic discipline.
Coverage increasingly reports petitions by their cumulative sign-up totals and by phone-based signing, which should rise if people are signing more often and more casually.

Early coverage frames petition activity as personal letter-writing to officials, while later coverage frames it as bulk automated email campaigns, suggesting signing feels more like a mass, low-effort appeal that people withdraw from.
Discussion of personal data and privacy increasingly comes with explicit refusals to hand over details to campaign sites, which should rise if people become more reluctant to sign at all.
In local planning disputes, residents shift from submitting paper objection forms to signing online on their phones, which would indicate growing ease and frequency of signing among those who engage.
Coverage increasingly describes petition emails and reminders as a nuisance, which should rise if people become more inclined to say they would never sign.
Coverage of petitions going viral on social media increases over time, reflecting more people encountering and signing petitions through shared links.
In housing and tenant coverage, mentions of petitions being ignored by landlords or councils increase, signalling a growing sense that signing achieves nothing (movement toward 'Not done').
Descriptions of how petitions are signed shift from paper-based methods toward one-step link and social sharing methods, which lower the effort of signing and favour 'Have done'.

In public services coverage, petitions move from being described as delivered to officials (implying a response) to being described as ignored, reflecting growing disillusionment and movement toward 'Not done'.
References to official government petition websites rise over time, indicating more frequent use of formal online petition platforms, which supports movement toward 'Have done'.

Coverage increasingly describes people actively boycotting, using present-participle and action phrasing rather than hypothetical talk, so actual participation language rises over time, consistent with a shift toward 'Have done'.

Coverage of anti-boycott legislation (laws barring state contracts with firms that boycott a country) rises over time, signaling a growing institutional push against boycotting and a population more likely to say they would never boycott.

Early coverage frames boycotting as a prospective option people are weighing, while later coverage reports completed personal disengagement from brands, indicating movement toward actual past participation, i.e. 'Have done'.

In sports and entertainment fandom, early coverage reports calls for boycotts of teams or sponsors, while later coverage reports fans explicitly ruling out boycotts, indicating movement toward 'Would never do'.
Coverage increasingly emphasizes that boycotts had no measurable effect on sales or outcomes, a skeptical framing that tends to discourage participation and shifts attitudes toward 'Would never do'.
Coverage of boycotts tied to long-running international political campaigns rises over the period, reflecting more people joining boycotts of specific companies.
Coverage describing boycott movements as fading or exhausted rises over the period, reflecting fewer people still participating.
Within fashion and apparel retail coverage, boycott mentions decline over the period as shoppers return to brands they had avoided.
Coverage shifts from describing people who pledged to boycott toward coverage describing people who actually refused to buy, indicating more people acting on boycotts.
In fuel and gas station coverage, language shifts from boycott calls toward reports of drivers actually avoiding pumps, indicating growing participation.

Coverage increasingly describes advancement as driven by favoritism and patronage rather than merit, so cronyism-style vocabulary rises over time, signaling a shift toward the belief that success depends on luck and connections.

In coverage of public-sector workers, language emphasizing steady, earned career progression and years of service rises over time, reflecting a stronger belief that sustained effort leads to a better life.

Descriptions of individual success shift from self-starter and earned-achievement framing toward inherited advantage and family wealth, indicating movement toward the view that luck and background determine outcomes.

Coverage of immigrant families moves from stories of being locked out and lacking a foothold toward stories of building businesses and futures through effort, reflecting growing confidence that hard work pays off.
Reciprocity-style sayings about effort being repaid appear more often over time, marking a rise in the conviction that the harder one works, the better one's life becomes.
Coverage of revolving-door appointments and lobbying by former ministers and officials rises over the period, signalling growing public doubt that senior officials act impartially (Direction A).
Early coverage frames officials through the satirical 'obstructive mandarin' image, while later coverage frames them through professional recognition of their work (Direction B).

Reporting on senior departures from the top of the Civil Service (permanent secretaries and Cabinet Office leadership) increases, with more stories of officials being pushed out or resigning, eroding confidence (Direction A).
Positive workforce-performance coverage about civil servants, such as engagement results and recognition of delivery teams, increases over time, pushing confidence upward (Direction B).

Coverage of ministers' relationship with officials shifts from describing trusted, independent advice to describing leaks, loyalty tests and advisers acting as yes-men, which undermines confidence (Direction A).
Coverage of women's organizations increasingly features the Women's March antisemitism controversy and its leaders, which would signal eroding public confidence (Direction A).
Rising use of rapid-response relief vocabulary in coverage of women-led groups would reflect growing public appreciation of their emergency work (Direction B).
Sexual assault hotlines and crisis lines run by women's groups increasingly appear alongside service-capacity failures, pointing to declining confidence (Direction A).
Coverage shifting from legacy women's social clubs and auxiliaries toward crisis-response networks would signal a move toward higher confidence (Direction B).
Among women's political action groups, coverage moving from endorsements and fundraising milestones to ethics and FEC complaints would signal declining confidence (Direction A).
Coverage of cross-border economic integration grows more frequent over time, reflecting a rising positive frame for North American trade that would push confidence toward 'A great deal'.

Within coverage of the original North American Free Trade Agreement, language about plant flight and low-wage assembly becomes more common, reflecting growing distrust that would move confidence toward 'None at all'.

Early coverage frames the agreement through labor and exploitation terms, while later coverage shifts toward exploitation-critique vocabulary, indicating an erosion of confidence toward 'None at all'.
Coverage of Mexican workers moves from exploitation framing to reform framing, consistent with rising confidence toward 'A great deal' as labor provisions are seen as improving outcomes.
Auto-sector coverage increasingly uses integration and production-efficiency terms, reflecting improving perceptions of the agreement's economic payoff and pushing confidence toward 'A great deal'.
Public skepticism toward charities grew over the period, which would show up as more articles using explicit distrust language about charitable giving.
Confidence in charities rose after pandemic-era relief work, which should increase coverage of community giving and volunteer response in relief-focused stories.
Coverage shifted from viral, celebrity-driven charity campaigns that were received warmly to stories about executive pay and fundraising controversies, which would signal declining confidence.
Faith-based charities moved from coverage of institutional abuse scandals to coverage of rebuilt community trust, which would signal rising confidence.
Regulatory enforcement against charities intensified, which would show up as more articles about tax-exempt status actions and watchdog findings, consistent with declining confidence.
Coverage of expert-led decision-making increasingly uses 'follow the data' and 'evidence-led' framing, signalling a shift toward favouring expert governance (Direction B).
Critical framing of expert rule as 'expertocracy' or 'ivory tower' governance increases, signalling a shift toward disapproval of expert-led government (Direction A).
Framing shifts from popular-mandate language to depictions of governance by unaccountable technocratic elites, signalling movement toward disapproval of expert rule (Direction A).
In drug and treatment approval coverage, mentions of the NICE-style regulator's clinical verdicts rise as the public appears more accepting of expert decisions (Direction B).

In coverage of rationing and drug access, framing moves from complaints about postcode lotteries and drug-company profits to praise of expert regulatory judgement, signalling movement toward approval of expert decisions (Direction B).
As the public sees more science-backed evidence and prizes recognizing research, average agreement that science and technology improve life should rise (Direction A).
Consumer frustration with connected devices that fail or lock users out should grow, pulling average agreement down toward disagreement (Direction B).
If coverage moves from overpromised hype toward demonstrated real-world results, agreement that technology delivers healthier, easier lives should rise (Direction A).

In urban transport, a shift from utopian talk about self-driving and smart cities toward documented congestion and rider injuries should lower agreement that technology makes daily life easier (Direction B).
Reports of rising healthspan and eradicated diseases should increase, reflecting growing belief that science improves health outcomes (Direction A).
Public optimism about science-driven progress rose as coverage of concrete, near-term technological achievements grew more frequent.
Pessimism about the next generation's prospects grew as coverage of school performance in the education sector increasingly reported declines.
Coverage shifted from forecasting inevitable decline toward reporting concrete clean-energy and space-launch successes, lifting belief that science opens future opportunities.
In health-care coverage, reporting moved from staffing shortages toward new treatments, which would make people more confident that science expands future opportunities.
Public distrust of technology grew as coverage increasingly focused on deepfakes, algorithmic harms, and surveillance, reducing belief that science will expand opportunity.
Pandemic-era home hobby boom: coverage of newly popular stay-at-home pastimes should rise, pushing the average answer toward 'Have done'.

Backyard gardening uptake: in coverage of home gardens, mentions of people who never grew food should give way to people who have started planting, indicating movement toward 'Have done'.
Live-event attendance decline: coverage describing people skipping concerts, theatre, or sporting events should rise, indicating movement toward 'Not done'.

Rising use of French-style laïcité and state religious-neutrality vocabulary signals growing public rejection of clerical interpretation of law (Direction B).

Coverage shifting from Shariah-compliance and religious-edict framing toward legal pluralism and civil-rights statute framing indicates movement against clerical law interpretation (Direction B).

In debates over human rights treaties, a shift from international-covenant language to references to religious law and ulema opinions indicates movement toward accepting religious interpretation of law (Direction A).

As the public increasingly treats elections as the only legitimate route to office, phrases asserting that power must be won at the ballot box should become more common, pushing the average toward 'essential'.
Religious-authority framings that reject electoral democracy as incompatible with divine or clerical rule should become more prevalent, moving the average toward 'against democracy'.
Earlier coverage framing leaders as chosen by appointment, elders, or party selection should give way to language of citizens directly selecting their rulers, indicating movement toward 'essential'.
Public-opinion coverage shifting from describing ordinary people as indifferent to elections toward reporting citizens demanding a vote should signal movement toward 'essential'.

Rising public fear of crime and lawlessness should make calls for a tough, military-backed response more common, moving attitudes toward accepting army action (direction A).
Discourse shifting from rights-based language toward order-based language signals growing acceptance of the army as a restorer of order (direction A).

Marriage and divorce coverage increasingly features explicit legal equality provisions for wives, reflecting rising endorsement of women's equal rights as essential.

Public engagement with mortality and the good life, shown by death-positive and end-of-life planning coverage, increases alongside more frequent self-reflection on life's purpose (Direction B).

Coverage of gaming as an escape from daily life and idle time grows as people think less often about meaning, so escapist gaming language should rise (Direction A).

Coverage of intensified or committed religious practice, such as daily prayer and retreats, becomes more common over time, pointing toward more frequent attendance.

Coverage increasingly emphasizes efforts to preserve existing marriages, such as reconciliation and counseling, reflecting renewed valuing of marital stability, which would move attitudes toward 'Never justifiable'.

Coverage moves from framing spousal beating as a private matter tolerated by reconciliation advice toward framing it as a criminal offence, indicating Direction B.

Distrust of neighbors rises as residents increasingly post or talk about excluding outsiders from private space, so 'no trespassing' and fencing language should grow more common.
Trust in neighbors rises as local food-assistance groups recruit residents to volunteer and donate, which should show more volunteer sign-up and drop-off language in food-bank coverage.

A shift from open, face-to-face neighborliness toward technology-mediated security should move coverage from open-door, outdoor-presence language to smart-lock and sensor language, indicating rising distrust.
In apartment and building settings, distrust of fellow residents grows as access-control and stranger-screening language replaces hallway greetings and shared building events.
Trust in neighbors rises as informal good-deed behaviors toward neighbors become more commonly reported, such as shoveling for others, watering plants, and taking in deliveries.
Coverage increasingly uses language of giving strangers the benefit of the doubt and good-faith assumptions about others, which would indicate rising trust in strangers.
Coverage increasingly uses home-security and property-crime language, which would indicate a drop in willingness to trust unfamiliar people at the door or on the street.
Discussion of doorbell cameras and neighborhood surveillance increasingly frames unfamiliar visitors as suspects, which would indicate falling trust in strangers.
Coverage of everyday interactions shifts from wariness toward strangers to openness and friendliness, which would indicate rising trust.
Coverage of bystanders and public emergencies shifts from describing people who ignored others to people who stepped in to help, which would indicate rising trust in strangers.

As intermarriage and multiracial families grow, coverage of mixed-heritage people with a native-born parent should increase, which would move answers toward 'No' for mothers.

Reporting on refugee resettlement and arrivals of new immigrants with families will grow, increasing the likelihood that respondents' mothers were immigrants.
In coverage of Latino and Asian American families, framing shifts from foreign-born mothers toward U.S.-born mothers, reflecting a growing native-born share of mothers and a move toward 'No'.
